questions.question: Show me something that looks like a tomato dinosaur!
questions.prompt:
You are generating questions for an object detection game for a 4-year-old child.
Available physical toys: Red Dino.
TARGET MLU (knowledge base): the child's mean length of utterance is about 5-6 words. Keep every question within that length.
Do NOT reuse any of these recently played questions:
  - Can you bring me a curved yellow fruit?
  - I'm looking for a tiny purple fruit!
  - Find something with little seeds on the outside!
  - Can you find a cool it toy?
  - Can you find a it toy?
  - Show me a it toy!
  - Can you bring me a red vehicle?
  - Find me a white vehicle please!
  - I'm looking for a dark black vehicle!
  - Can you find a cool ocean-colored dinosaur toy?
  - Show me a dinosaur that matches the sky!
  - Bring me a dinosaur the color of water!
  - Can you find a dinosaur that looks like grass?
  - Show me a dinosaur the color of a frog!
  - I'm looking for a leafy-colored dinosaur toy!
  - Can you find a firetruck-colored vehicle toy?
  - Show me a vehicle that looks like a strawberry!
  - Bring me a bright apple-colored vehicle!
  - Can you find a snowy-colored vehicle toy?
  - Show me a vehicle that looks like a cloud!
Generate exactly 3 DIFFERENT inference-style requests for EACH target that let the child figure out THAT target without naming it.
Do this for ALL 1 target objects listed below (3 questions in total — exactly 3 per target):
  1. Red Dino

HARD RULE — a question must NEVER contain the name of ITS target or ANY other toy. It must contain NONE of these words:
  Red Dino
Refer to the target only as "it", "something", or "one". The child must INFER which object is meant.
CLUE STYLE — each spoken question must be ONE of these two kinds:
  (a) An ASSOCIATION / FUNCTION clue (what animal eats it, what you do with it, where you find it). These are the best clues and may stand alone. Good: "Get me something rabbits love to eat!"
  (b) A PHYSICAL-PROPERTY clue (color/shape/size/texture). When you describe properties you MUST also name the object's CATEGORY (fruit, vegetable, animal, ...) so the child knows what kind of thing to look for. Good: "I want a skinny, bright orange vegetable!" BAD: "I want something skinny and bright orange!" (no category word).
HOW THE CHILD ANSWERS — the child finds the matching toy, picks it up, and holds it up to the robot's camera. So every request must ask the child to find and SHOW or BRING the object — never to merely point at it.
PHRASING VARIETY — vary the sentence opener across the whole set; do NOT start most questions with "Get me" or "I want". Rotate among natural openers such as "Can you find ...", "Let's find ...", "Can you bring me ...", "Show me ...", "Where is ...", "I'm looking for ...", "Which one is ...", "Find ...".
CRITERIA RULE — each "criteria" is a short concrete descriptor: at most ONE adjective plus the CATEGORY noun (e.g. "orange vegetable", "red fruit"); never a function phrase, compound, or multi-object.
UNIQUENESS RULE — a target's 3 questions must each use a DIFFERENT property or association, and every question must fit ONLY its own target among the toys (use a distinguishing feature no other listed toy shares).
Use simple, clear language appropriate for ages 4-6.
Example object: {"target": "carrot", "question": "Can you find something rabbits love to eat?", "criteria": "orange vegetable"}

Return ONLY a JSON object, no other text:
{"questions": [ {"target": "<exact toy name>", "question": "<sentence, contains no toy name>", "criteria": "<one noun + at most one adjective>"}, ... ]}
The array MUST hold exactly 3 objects: 3 for each target.
